result.lens: Layering — does anything read across a boundary it should not (F1: analytical usage reads only DAR; F2: DAR reads only DAB; F3: DAB reads only DAS)
result.summary: Every actual read in this slice stays inside its layer: DAR names only objects in the `dab` schema, the mappings name only `das__staged.orders`/`das__staged.customers`, the destination executes nothing but each question's `uss.sql`, and `das/sql/customers.sql` is pure extraction with no interpretation. On the sharp question — `dar/uss/_bridge.sql` reading `dab."v_ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER"`, which INNER JOINs `dab__meta.atom_contx_desc` — I do not believe this breaks F2. Against: F2 is worded "DAR reads only DAB", and if `dab__meta` is a fourth thing rather than part of DAB, DAR now reaches it. For: every artefact in the repository that enumerates DAB's schemas includes `dab__meta` (README.md:9, .claude/skills/adss/SKILL.md:14, src/adss/names.py:26 where `Schema.layer` maps it to `Layer.DAB`); the harm F2 names is "reaches past the business layer to a source", and `atom_contx_desc` is not a source but the business model's own name registry — I read it and `val_str` holds `ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER`, `ORDER_FREIGHT_CHARGE`, i.e. the identifiers straight out of `dab/model.yaml`, so the read is what makes `rel_name = 'ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER'` possible instead of `type_key = 1`; and a transitive-closure reading of F2 would already have condemned slice 1, since `dab.view_ORDER_hist` composes from `dab.ORDER_desc`, which is populated from `dab__stage`, which is populated from `das__staged`. DAR names one object, it is in `dab`, and what it joins to internally is DAB's own composition. The three findings are about what is written down and what is pinned, not about a misplaced read.

findings.finding: The checks suite now spans all three layers and nothing in the repository states that a conformance check may sit outside F1. F1 has exactly one written exemption — conventions §10 requires the control query to read `das__staged.<table>__current` — and no rule generalises it. This slice adds the first committed check files that read `dab.*` directly, so the unwritten exemption became visible in reviewable artefacts for the first time.
findings.evidence: blueprint.md:50 states F1 as an absolute: "Analytical usage reads only DAR." conventions.md:176 describes the second suite only as "Assertions about what the built warehouse actually contains" — nothing about layers. conventions.md:238 is the only rule that authorises a check to read another layer, and only for one query: "The staged query reads `das__staged.<table>__current` and must not mention `dab` or `dar__uss`." `git ls-tree --name-only 28a6065 checks/` returns only `checks/README.md`, `checks/orders__clock.sql`, `checks/orders__key.sql` — both SQL files read `das__staged`. The new `checks/order_is_placed_by_customer__loaded.sql:6` reads `FROM dab."v_ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER" AS pair`, and `__resolves.sql:3-4` reads `dar__uss._bridge` / `dar__uss.customer`. conventions.md:254-255: "What is not on the list: a quiet exception. That is how a system of conventions turns into a set of stories about why each file is the way it is."
findings.fix: One sentence in conventions §6 saying that the checks suite verifies the system rather than consuming it, so it reads whatever layer the assertion is about, and that F1 governs analytical usage — destinations and questions' `uss.sql` — not verification. That is the §11 recourse ("Clarify this page") and costs nothing; the alternative reading would require a deviations.md entry, which is worse and, I think, wrong.

findings.finding: Nothing mechanically enforces F2 over the generated DAR SQL. `names.py` exists, by its own docstring, to give a flow check something to check against, but `Layer` and `Schema.layer` have no call sites anywhere. The only flow enforcement in the repository is `check_question`, which covers the two question SQL bodies. Pre-existing, but the exposure grew here: DAR's DAB read set went from one object family (`dab."view_<E>_hist"`) to two, adding `dab."v_<edge>"`.
findings.evidence: src/adss/names.py:1 — "The names this system owns. One place, so a flow check has something closed to check against." `grep -rn "\.layer\b|Layer(" --include=*.py src tests` returns only the two definition lines in names.py — zero uses. src/adss/question.py:116-123 is the only flow assertion: `for forbidden in ("das__", "dab.", "dab__", "read_parquet"): if forbidden in answer: raise QuestionError(...)`. `uv run adss dar generate --check` exits 0, but it only proves the committed file equals the generator's output — it says nothing about which schemas the generator emits.
findings.fix: A machinery test over `_generate(project)`'s output asserting that the only schema-qualified references outside `dar__uss` are `dab.` — neutral fixtures, no business vocabulary needed. It would have made the `dab__meta` question above answerable by running something rather than by reading a view definition.

findings.finding: ADR 0006 rests DAR's safety on pinning, but the one property that makes `v_<edge>` the right object to read — that it is the raw, unranked, unfiltered pairs — is the one engine behaviour not pinned. If a vendor release added ranking inside that view, the as-of rule ADR 0006 spends generated SQL to own would silently revert to the vendor's "as of now", and every check and both questions would still pass.
findings.evidence: ADR 0006 (Consequences): "Bad, because `v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` is an engine-internal object with no compatibility promise, like every other object here. The pinning checks are what turn a vendor change into a failure instead of an empty column." The pinning loop in src/adss/checks.py:71-117 covers `<E>_focal`, `<E>_idfr`, `view_<E>_with_rel` and `<E>_desc`; nothing looks at `v_<edge>`. Read-only from the warehouse, the current definition has no QUALIFY and no `row_st` filter: `CREATE VIEW dab.v_ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER AS SELECT an.ORDER_key, an.CUSTOMER_key, bn.val_str AS rel_name, ... FROM dab.ORDER_CUSTOMER_x AS an INNER JOIN dab__meta.atom_contx_desc AS bn ON ((an.type_key = CAST(bn.atom_contx_key AS BIGINT)))`. The change would be invisible today: `select count(*) from dab."v_ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER"` returns 830 against 830 orders, all `row_st = 'Y'`, so the edge carries no history at all — `__loaded` would still find pairs, `__one_target` would still find no ties, and `uv run adss check` reports 18 PASS either way.
findings.fix: Add one behaviour pin beside the existing four: assert that `dab."v_<edge>"` returns the same row count as `dab."<SRC>_<TGT>_x"` (830 = 830 today), which is what "unranked and unfiltered" looks like from outside and is the assumption the generated as-of join is built on.

checkedAndFound: dar/uss/_bridge.sql, order.sql, customer.sql reference only the `dab` schema — `grep -rn "dab\.|dab__|das__" dar/ destinations/app.py docs/questions/*/uss.sql` returns four lines, all `dab."view_<E>_hist"` or `dab."v_ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER"`. No `dab__stage`, no `dab__meta`, no `das__` anywhere in DAR.

The transitive `dab__meta` read is genuinely new to this slice — I checked, and `dab.view_ORDER_hist` (which slice 1 read) resolves entirely against `dab.ORDER_desc` with hardcoded `type_key` values (17, 18, 9, 10) and never touches `dab__meta`. So the question the lens raises is real, not a rediscovery. I still judge it inside DAB, for the reasons in the summary.

The `dab__meta` INNER JOIN does not silently drop pairs here: `dab."ORDER_CUSTOMER_x"` holds 830 rows and `dab."v_ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER"` holds 830, all with `rel_name = 'ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER'`. And even if metadata went missing, the bridge's join is LEFT, so an order would lose its customer key rather than its row.

No single check file crosses a boundary — the lens brief's premise is slightly off. `__loaded` and `__one_target` read only `dab.*`; `__resolves` reads only `dar__uss.*`. It is the suite that spans layers, not any one statement.

destinations/app.py touches nothing but `dar__uss` via each question's `uss_sql` (line 105, `warehouse.execute(q.uss_sql)`), and `check_question` (src/adss/question.py:113-123) refuses any `uss.sql` mentioning `das__`, `dab.`, `dab__` or `read_parquet`. `docs/questions/02/.../uss.sql` reads `dar__uss._bridge`, `dar__uss._calendar`, `dar__uss.customer` only.

app.py also reads `dab/model.yaml` and `dab/uss.yaml` for the glossary (lines 74-76). That is definitions, not data, and conventions §1.2 names the app explicitly: "Everything else — contracts, questions, the generated layer, the app — references these." It is unchanged from 28a6065 (`git show 28a6065:destinations/app.py` lines 52-55 are identical).
The marimo session cache `destinations/__marimo__/session/app.py.json` contains no `dab.` or `das__` reference.

dab/mappings/*.yaml read `das__staged` only — `table: das__staged.customers`, `table: das__staged.orders`, and the relationship's `source_table: das__staged.orders`, which M6 forces byte-identical to its group's table (src/adss/mapping.py:241-248). The compiled `dab/mappings/order-mapping.json` confirms the engine sees the same single table.

The new relationship block introduces no reach M1 or M5 would forbid: `target_transformation_expression: customer_id` is a bare column of `das__staged.orders` (das/sql/orders.sql:46). Note that `check_mapping`'s M5 regex is applied to `table.expressions` only (src/adss/mapping.py:163-168), never to `edge.target_expression`; the guarantee in practice comes from M6's `key_shape` comparison instead, which reduces the expression to `?` and so admits only a bare identifier when the target key is one. The property holds; the rule cited for it in ADR 0006 is not the rule enforcing it.

das/sql/customers.sql records rather than interprets: eleven `payload ->> '$.X'` extractions with source spellings preserved, no CASE, no coalesce, no derivation. The `__current` view's `row_number()` over `extracted_at` is the mechanical latest-per-key that conventions §1.1 mandates for every contract, not a business rule. The contract format cannot express logic — `read_contract` refuses forbidden keys (src/adss/contract.py:110-121) and forces `target_name` to be the mechanical snake_case of `source_path` (lines 137-143).

Nothing in DAS or DAB references a layer above it: `grep -rn "das__|dar__" dab/*.yaml dab/mappings/*.yaml` returns only the three `das__staged` lines; `grep -rn "dab|dar__" das/sql/*.sql das/contracts/*.yaml` returns only two prose comments pointing at dab/model.yaml as the place meaning lives.

Ran read-only: `uv run pytest -q` (112 passed), `uv run adss check` (18 PASS, 0 FAIL), `uv run adss dar generate --check` (rc 0), `uv run adss das unpack --check` (rc 0), `uv run ruff check` (clean), `uv run sqlfluff lint dar/uss checks docs/questions` (clean). `git status --porcelain` is empty — I wrote nothing in the repository.

result.lens: conventions — does the slice obey the rules this repository set itself?
result.summary: The built artefacts of this slice conform closely: no source name leaks into dab/model.yaml, no data vocabulary reaches src/ or tests/ (checked mechanically, atom by atom, against every id in the model and every column in both contracts), FREIGHT_ORDERS_AMOUNT satisfies every clause of §2, the generated DAR SQL obeys §1.3 and §3, and ruff, sqlfluff, yamllint --strict, 112 pytest tests, 18 data checks and `adss dar generate --check` are all clean. Everything I found is prose that the code has moved past: README.md still says question 2 is "not started", ADR 0004 still repeats the `_with_rel` claim the probe disproved, and conventions §1.4 M6 still states a rule ("exactly", "its group's table") that src/adss/mapping.py deliberately does not enforce. None of it is a data or correctness defect, so none of it blocks; all of it is a page that now disagrees with the system it governs.

findings.finding: The repository's front page is stale about the slice it just delivered. Line 19 still says "Slice 1 is green: one business question answered end to end", and the Slices table at line 43 still says question 2 is "not started". Both are contradicted by artefacts committed in this same slice.
findings.evidence: grep -n on README.md returns `19:Slice 1 is green: one business question answered end to end, through all three layers, and` and `43:| 2 | What freight did we pay per customer country and order quarter? | not started |`. Against that: docs/questions/README.md:18 marks question 2 `| green |`, docs/questions/02-freight-per-customer-country-and-quarter/question.md front matter says `status: green`, and `uv run adss check` prints `PASS  q02: the source and the star schema agree`. Commit 61f41d7 updated docs/questions/README.md and left README.md untouched.
findings.fix: Update both lines in the same commit that flips a question to green. The deeper issue is that README.md keeps a second copy of the question-status table that docs/questions/README.md owns — conventions.md's own preamble ("a convention that exists both as prose and as a linter config exists twice, the two copies disagree") argues for the README pointing at that list rather than restating it, which it already does two lines later.

findings.finding: ADR 0004 still states as observed fact the claim this slice's probe disproved: "`view_<entity>_with_rel` carries no relationship keys despite its name." ADR 0006 corrects that claim where ADR 0002 makes it, and commit 3650b66 corrects it in both skills, but the copy in ADR 0004 was missed — in the very file this slice edited (015f9c5) for a different stale claim, and in the record that says of itself it is "where someone will look for it".
findings.evidence: `grep -n with_rel docs/adr/0004-daana-cli-is-the-dab-engine.md` → `36:populated. \`view_<entity>_with_rel\` carries no relationship keys despite its name. And if the`. ADR 0004:93-95 says "That is recorded here rather than in the DAR record because it is a fact about this engine on this platform, and it is where someone will look for it." The claim is false at HEAD: docs/adr/0006:37-44 records the probe, src/adss/checks.py:86-100 asserts the target-side view equals the plain view plus the source entity's columns, and `uv run adss check` prints `PASS  dab.view_CUSTOMER_with_rel is what a target side looks like`. ADR 0006's correction section (line 134) is headed "Corrections to ADR 0002" and names only 0002.
findings.fix: Extend ADR 0006's corrections section to name and quote ADR 0004:36 as well, per the policy this slice wrote at docs/adr/README.md:5-7 ("corrected in the record that found it wrong, named and quoted, rather than quietly rewritten where it stands"). Line 93's "Not `_focal`, not `_idfr`, not `_with_rel`" is still sound guidance and needs nothing.

findings.finding: M6's stated rule and its enforced rule differ, and the page was not clarified. conventions.md M6 says a relationship's "target expression mirrors the target entity's own key expression exactly", with the why "a differently spelled key produces pairs that join to nothing". The implementation deliberately compares shape with the names stripped out, and a test asserts that a differently spelled key is accepted. The code's reasoning is better than the page's — a foreign key is routinely named differently from the primary key it points at, and it is the casting that decides the VARCHAR — but conventions.md §11 says the recourse is to clarify that page, "in force immediately, for everyone", and conventions.md is untouched in this slice.
findings.evidence: docs/conventions.md:93 reads `| M6 | A relationship's \`id\` is \`<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>\`; its \`source_table\` is byte-identical to its group's \`table\`; its target expression mirrors the target entity's own key expression exactly. | A mismatched \`source_table\` is skipped silently, and a differently spelled key produces pairs that join to nothing. ... | Hard rule |`. src/adss/mapping.py:176-183 docstring: "It is the *shape* that has to match, not the spelling: a foreign key column is routinely named differently from the primary key it points at." tests/fixtures/mappings/good_child_renamed_key.yaml targets `points_at` against a parent keyed `parent_id`, and tests/test_relationship_rules.py:73 `test_the_key_shape_is_compared_and_not_the_column_name` asserts it passes. `git diff 28a6065..HEAD --stat` lists no change to docs/conventions.md; the divergence is disclosed only in commit cee95ff's body.
findings.fix: Clarify M6 on conventions.md: the target expression must mirror the target key's *shape* — same casting and same separators — and may name a different column, with the current why replaced (a differently spelled column is normal; a differently cast one is what joins to nothing). One artefact, per the page's own opening argument.

findings.finding: A slice-1 ADR was edited in slice 2, and the rule permitting it was written six minutes later, on a different page from the one that carries the rule it amends. conventions.md §8 is a hard rule — an ADR "is superseded by a new file rather than edited", with exactly one exception, "within the slice that wrote it, before any code depends on it". ADR 0004 is a slice-1 record with code depending on it, so the edit is outside that exception as conventions.md states it. The new carve-out for Confirmation sections lives only in docs/adr/README.md, so the exception set for §8 now exists in two documents that do not agree.
findings.evidence: `git log --format='%h %ad %s' --date=iso --reverse` for the slice: `015f9c5 2026-09-07 22:35:46 docs(adr): say what pins the engine...` touching only docs/adr/0004-daana-cli-is-the-dab-engine.md, then `55edbd7 2026-09-07 22:41:42` adding docs/adr/README.md:9-12 "**The Confirmation section is the one exception** ... It is edited to match the checks". docs/conventions.md:207-208 still lists only the within-the-slice exception. docs/conventions.md:246-247 (§11) says the recourse is "Clarify this page", and 254-255: "What is not on the list: a quiet exception."
findings.fix: Add the Confirmation-section exception to conventions.md §8 (the ADR README can then reference it rather than state it), and, where an ADR edit is the intended path, land the clarification before the edit it licenses — the same ordering §7 already demands of an ADR and its code.

findings.finding: The source_table check is one scope wider than M6 describes. M6 says source_table is "byte-identical to its group's `table`", and the error message says "not byte-identical to any table in its group" — but the set compared against is every table in the whole mapping, because read_mapping flattens tables across all mapping_groups (mapping.py:96-111). A relationship declared in one group that names a table belonging to another group passes the check and would still be the silent skip M6 exists to catch. Nothing in the repository exercises it today: every mapping has exactly one group.
findings.evidence: src/adss/mapping.py:241 `tables = {table.table for table in mapping.tables}` where `mapping.tables` is built at 96-111 with `for group in document["mapping_groups"] for table in group["tables"]`. Demonstrated: a fixture at /tmp/m6/two_groups.yaml declaring group_one (table das__staged.child) and group_two (table das__staged.child_extra, relationships naming source_table das__staged.child) is accepted — `uv run python -c "...check_relationships(...)"` printed `ACCEPTED: relationship in group_two names a table that belongs to group_one`.
findings.fix: Scope the comparison to the group the relationship is declared in, or, if mapping-wide is what is meant, say so in M6 and in the message. Either way the message and the rule should describe the same set.

findings.finding: D-0001's review paragraph still frames the assertion gap in slice-1 terms, in the slice that added the first edge. The register says it is read at the start of every slice and each open entry checked "against whether its argument is still being carried on assertion"; a reader arriving in slice 3 is told the walk is unexercised because slice 1 had one entity, which no longer describes the state of the argument. ADR 0006 is honest that the property is still asserted and first provable in slice 4 — that is what the register should now say.
findings.evidence: docs/deviations.md:45-47: "D-0001's justification rests on a walk over many-to-one edges, which slice 1's single entity does not exercise at all." `git diff 28a6065..HEAD --stat` lists no change to docs/deviations.md. ADR 0006's Confirmation closes: "What this slice still does not prove is the fan-out property itself. Both entities here are at the same grain ... The first measure at a finer grain arrives in slice 4 ... ADR 0002 asserted this property in slice 1 and it is still asserted now."
findings.fix: Update D-0001's review sentence to say the walk now has one edge but both entities are at one grain, so the fan-trap property remains asserted until slice 4 — the exit condition and status are unchanged and correct.

findings.finding: §1.2's first hard rule cannot be satisfied by a relationship, which only becomes visible now that the first one exists. It says identifiers are UPPER_SNAKE_CASE "with `id` and `name` holding the identical string", but a relationship in dab/model.yaml carries only `name: IS_PLACED_BY`; its id, ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER, is composed from source, name and target, and the engine's relationship grammar has no `id` field at all. So id and name are necessarily different strings for every relationship. M6 (line 93) already describes relationship ids correctly; line 53 does not.
findings.evidence: docs/conventions.md:53 as quoted. dab/model.yaml:104-111 declares the relationship with `name: IS_PLACED_BY` and no `id`. src/adss/model.py:89-92: `@property def id(self) -> str: ... return f"{self.source_entity_id}_{self.name}_{self.target_entity_id}"`. ADR 0006 quotes the engine's own error listing the whole grammar: "Valid fields are: name, definition, description, source, target, source_entity_id, target_entity_id, type" — no id.
findings.fix: Scope line 53's id/name clause to entities and attributes, and let M6 carry the relationship case.

checkedAndFound: §1.2, no source name in dab/model.yaml — clean. I compared every id, name, definition and description in the model against every source_path and target_name in both contracts programmatically: no exact match, and every source-flavoured word was renamed (CustomerId→CUSTOMER_CODE, CompanyName→TRADING_NAME, Country→BASED_IN_COUNTRY, ShipCountry→DESTINATION_COUNTRY, OrderId→ORDER_NUMBER).

FREIGHT_CHARGE is not a §1.2 violation, on the rule's own why. The test the why sets is whether the name would have to change if the source were replaced — "a source name in it means the dependency was moved rather than broken". It would not: the business pays freight whichever system records it. The rule also cannot mean "no string the source also uses", or ORDER and CUSTOMER would both be violations (Orders, Customers, CustomerId), which would leave the model unable to name its own subjects. And the DAB name is not the source's: the column is `Freight`, the attribute is FREIGHT_CHARGE, qualified and given a business definition ("What the business paid to have this order carried to its destination"). §1.2's guideline "prefer the word the business already uses" points the same way — the persona in docs/questions/02.../question.md is a logistics manager asking "what freight did we pay". The same argument covers COUNTRY inside DESTINATION_COUNTRY and BASED_IN_COUNTRY.

§2, FREIGHT_ORDERS_AMOUNT against every clause — passes. Three parts in order (freight / orders / amount); entity part plural; no scope or aggregation word (no total_, sum_, count_of_, _ytd); `amount` is one of the three units the rule names; not a ratio (dab/uss.yaml:29-30 declares aggregate sum over FREIGHT_CHARGE, and the question divides nothing); no abbreviation; self-explanatory. It is exactly the shape of the page's own worked example, `sum_revenue` → `revenue_order_lines_amount`. The whole name survives into `_measure__order__freight_orders_amount` per §1.3.

§5 and §6, no data vocabulary under src/ or tests/ — clean, checked mechanically rather than by eye. I built the atom list from every entity, attribute, relationship, event and measure id in dab/model.yaml and dab/uss.yaml plus every source_path and target_name in both contracts, and searched every file under src/ and tests/ (including fixtures). Zero hits for customer, freight, country, ship, trading, based, charge, placed, destination-as-a-business-word, company, region, postal, phone, fax, via, employee. The only hits are machinery collisions: `order` in ORDER BY / `ordered` / the SQL reserved-word list in src/adss/names.py:8 (which is unchanged since 28a6065), `quarter` in the calendar emitter src/adss/uss.py:376-383 (also unchanged since 28a6065, and §1.3 names the calendar as the object the generator invents whole), `count`, `date`, `name`, `number`, `required`, `code`, and `destination`, which §5 itself lists as a machinery word.

The new test fixtures are genuinely neutral. tests/fixtures/dab/model.yaml adds NEIGHBOUR ("a thing that is only ever pointed at") alongside PARENT and CHILD, with two edges POINTS_AT and SITS_BESIDE; the six new mapping fixtures use child/parent/neighbour columns only. tests/test_relationship_rules.py names nothing from the business in any test name or assertion.

§1.3, DAR naming — clean. Objects snake_case singular (`customer`, and `dar__uss."order"` quoted, not abbreviated around); key columns `customer_key`/`order_key`; attribute columns the lower-cased identifier unchanged; structural columns all leading-underscore (`_stage`, `_event`, `_event_date`, `_is_current`, `_observed_at`, `_measure__…`); calendar columns bare, as the rule's stated exception; every column read from a DAB view named explicitly, no `SELECT *`; the inherited key joined LEFT and never given an invented member.

§1.4 M1-M5 and M7 on both mappings — conform: both read das__staged objects, one primary_keys entry each, FULL_LOG, extracted_at, no expression reaching past its row, at least one attribute each. M6's other two clauses hold on the real mapping: the id ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER matches `<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>`, source_table `das__staged.orders` is byte-identical to the group's table, and the target expression `customer_id` is in fact byte-identical to customer-mapping.yaml's `primary_keys: [customer_id]`, so the repository's own data satisfies even the strict reading of M6.
§1.2's relationship-name rule — the name reads as a sentence, ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER, which is the convention's own worked example.

§7 — branch is `claude/adss-slice-02-freight-per-customer-country-and-quarter`, the question's slug. All nine commit subjects are conventional with allowed types and scopes (fix/docs/feat × dab/adr/das/dar/questions/skills), imperative, lower case, no trailing period. Four run 86-89 characters against the "about 72" guideline, but slice 1 already ran to 83, so it is the repository's habit rather than this slice's departure.

§7's ADR-before-code rule holds: ADR 0006 landed at 22:41 (55edbd7), was amended at 22:43 (80d3a08), and the first code that implements it landed at 22:56 (421afc9). The amendment is honest — it is inside the writing slice with nothing yet depending on it, which is the one case conventions §8 permits, and 80d3a08's message says exactly that ("I wrote 0006 from part of the probe's report and committed it ... a record that is right by luck is not right"). It adds findings and strengthens the enforcement (only-open-pairs, the ver_tmstp tiebreak, the cardinality-cannot-be-declared argument) rather than reversing anything.

The ADR 0002 corrections are handled as the repository says they should be: not edited in place, corrected in ADR 0006 under a named heading with both claims quoted (docs/adr/0006:134-152), 0002 explicitly not superseded because its decision stands, and the mis-observed check replaced with a stronger one that passes on the real warehouse for both a source-side and a target-side entity.

The dab skill's false claim is fixed at HEAD. Commit 3650b66 rewrote .claude/skills/dab/SKILL.md:63-76 to say `view_<entity>_with_rel` is a passthrough on a source side and a fanned-out join on a target side, and added where relationship keys actually come from, the never-retracted null foreign key, and type_key's instability; .claude/skills/dar/SKILL.md:62-71 matches. It landed after the code that relies on it, which no rule forbids — §7's ordering rule is about ADRs.

result.lens: The inheritance mechanism — does the generated SQL do what ADR 0006 says it does?
result.summary: I checked every claim ADR 0006 makes against the emitted `dar/uss/_bridge.sql`, the generator that writes it, and the real warehouse, and then replayed the emitted SQL verbatim against scratch DuckDB databases holding the shapes this recording does not contain. Seven of the eight mechanical claims hold and I proved each one by making the opposite case: the pair source, the LEFT join, `row_number()` over a deterministic tiebreak, the as-of predicate on the observation time (not on now, not on the event date), the `row_st` filter, and matching by `rel_name` are all correct and all load-bearing. All three generated relationship checks pass on the real build and all three can be made to fail. One thing is not as the ADR describes: the as-of resolution is partitioned by the source key rather than by the bridge row, so the property the ADR spends its whole decision buying — that the rule survives a stage keeping more than the latest version — does not hold in the emitted SQL. It is latent today and does not affect this slice's answer.

findings.finding: The inherited key is resolved per source KEY, not per bridge ROW. `_inherit_cte` ranks with `PARTITION BY revision.{source.key_column}` and `_stage_cte` joins the result back on `{entity.key_column}` alone, so the CTE collapses to one parent per order regardless of how many versions of that order the stage retains, and every retained version then receives that single parent. ADR 0006's stated reason for choosing `_observed_at` over `now` is exactly this case: "it is what keeps the rule stated at the level of a bridge row rather than at the level of a table, so it survives a stage that keeps more than the latest version, which is what a snapshot event and a `_is_current = FALSE` row will both need." It does not survive it. This is latent, not live: `_version_cte` (uss.py:184-187) always QUALIFYs to one version per key and `read_uss` refuses `kind: snapshot` (uss.py:140-146), so no bridge today has two rows for one key. Nothing in the suite would catch it when that changes — `test_an_inherited_key_is_the_one_in_force_when_the_row_was_observed` (tests/test_uss.py:200-207) is a regex over the predicate's text, and the predicate text stays correct while the partition is wrong.
findings.evidence:
I ran the committed `dar/uss/_bridge.sql` verbatim against a scratch DuckDB, changing only one thing: deleting the QUALIFY inside `placed__version` so the stage retains both versions of one order (the snapshot / `_is_current = FALSE` shape). Data: order O1 observed 2026-01-10 and again 2026-02-10; pairs O1->CA effective 2026-01-05 and O1->CZ effective 2026-02-05. Output:
('O1', 2026-01-10 00:00:00, 'CZ')
('O1', 2026-02-10 00:00:00, 'CZ')
The January-observed row inherits the February customer — the exact re-pointing ADR 0006 refuses the engine's own ranked view for. With the QUALIFY in place (i.e. the shipped SQL against the shipped shape) the same scratch harness gives the right answer for every case: O3, observed 2026-01-10 with pairs CA at 2026-01-05 and CZ at 2026-01-20, resolves to 'CA'. Script and patched SQL: /tmp/lens/multi.duckdb, /tmp/lens/patched.sql.
findings.fix: Partition the inherit CTE by the inheriting row, not by its key: `PARTITION BY revision.{key}, revision._observed_at`, carry `_observed_at` out of the CTE alongside the two keys, and join it back in `_stage_cte` on `({key}, _observed_at)`. Then add a machinery test whose fixture stage yields two versions of one key with a pair change between them — otherwise the invariant is still only asserted.

findings.finding: `bridge_columns`'s docstring says "A model change appends; it never rearranges." It does rearrange. Key columns are emitted in `dab/model.yaml` entity order (`entity_ids`, uss.py:291), so an additive model change — a new entity plus a new edge, blueprint B7's canonical safe change — that is not written at the end of `model.yaml` shifts every existing key column right. Nothing guards it: the "bridge matches its published column contract" check derives `expected` from the same `bridge_columns()` call that generated the built table, so both sides move together and it still passes, and `test_the_key_columns_follow_the_model_order_not_the_declaration_order` (tests/test_uss.py:159-167) reverses the *events*, never the model's entities. The `entity_keys` docstring is candid that the check cannot catch a rearrangement; `bridge_columns`'s is not. Practical impact today is small — the question SQL and the destination read by name, and conventions §3 forbids `SELECT *` — so this is the docstring promising an invariant the code does not hold, not a live defect.
findings.evidence: Against the real model: `bridge_columns` gives (..., '_observed_at', 'order_key', 'customer_key', ...). Reversing the entities in a /tmp copy of `dab/model.yaml` gives (..., '_observed_at', 'customer_key', 'order_key', ...) — transposed, same types, and `bridge_sql` differs. Adding a purely new entity AGENT with a new ORDER->AGENT edge, written before ORDER in the file, gives (..., '_observed_at', 'agent_key', 'order_key', 'customer_key', ...): an additive change that moved both existing key columns.
findings.fix: Either correct the docstring to say what is actually true (the contract is model order, so where an entity is written in `model.yaml` is part of the published contract), or make the order independent of file position — first mention by the walk, with new entities appended — and add a test that an entity inserted at the front of a fixture model leaves the existing key columns in place.

checkedAndFound: 1. Pair source. `dar/uss/_bridge.sql:23` reads `LEFT JOIN dab."v_ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER" AS pair`. `grep -rn 'view_|_with_rel|type_key|ORDER_CUSTOMER_x' dar/ checks/` returns only `view_ORDER_hist` / `view_CUSTOMER_hist` (the entity history views) — no `view_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>`, no `_with_rel`, no pair table, no `type_key` anywhere in the generated layer. Confirmed the object is what the ADR describes: `duckdb_views()` shows `v_ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER` is `ORDER_CUSTOMER_x` INNER JOINed to `dab__meta.atom_contx_desc` for `rel_name`, unranked and unfiltered, while `view_ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER` is `SELECT * FROM dab.f_order_customer_x()`.

2. LEFT join, proven not just read. Replayed the committed `_bridge.sql` verbatim on a scratch DuckDB: order O2 with no pair row at all kept its bridge row with `customer_key` NULL; O6, whose only pair becomes effective after the order was observed, also kept its row with a NULL key. 6 orders in, 6 bridge rows out, freight summing to the true 210. The `row_st = 'Y'` and `rel_name` predicates sit in the ON clause, not the WHERE, so they filter which pair is eligible without converting the join to an inner one.

3. Ranking and tiebreak. `row_number()`, never `rank()`. Order O4 (two open pairs, same eff_tmstp, same ver_tmstp, different customers — the ADR's CH5 case) produced exactly one bridge row, 'CB', the lower target key; `rank()` there would have produced two and doubled that order's freight. O5 (same eff_tmstp, later ver_tmstp) resolved to the later version, so `ver_tmstp DESC` is load-bearing and correctly placed ahead of the key. The full tiebreak is `eff_tmstp DESC, ver_tmstp DESC, "CUSTOMER_key" ASC` — deterministic in value even if the whole triple ever tied.

4. As-of predicate, and both ways it could have been subtly wrong. `revision._observed_at >= pair.eff_tmstp`, where `_observed_at` is `view_ORDER_hist.eff_tmstp` and the mapping sets `entity_effective_timestamp_expression: extracted_at` (M4) — so it is the observation time. Not as of now: scratch order O3, observed 2026-01-10 with pairs CA at 2026-01-05 and CZ at 2026-01-20, inherits CA, whereas the engine's own current view would give CZ. Not as of the event date: in the warehouse `_event_date` spans 1996-07-04 to 1998-05-06 while every pair's eff_tmstp is 2026-09-07 22:11:09.111026, so an event-date predicate would null all 830 keys. The `>=` boundary is required rather than cosmetic — order and pair share that timestamp exactly, so a strict `>` would also have nulled all 830, and `__resolves` would not have caught it (it only inspects non-null keys); the question's acceptance query would.
5. `row_st = 'Y'` is filtered, in the join condition. Scratch order O1 had a later pair with `row_st = 'N'` pointing at CN and still resolved to C1.

6. Matched by `rel_name`, never by `type_key`. `pair.rel_name = 'ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER'` at _bridge.sql:26; scratch order O1's later pair under a different rel_name was ignored. `type_key` appears in no generated file.

7. Fan-out. This slice does not prove the property, it only fails to disprove it, exactly as ADR 0006 says: 830 orders, 830 pair rows, one customer each, both entities at one grain — `select count(*), count(distinct order_key) from dar__uss._bridge` gives (830, 830). What the code does guarantee at any grain along one edge: the inherit CTE reduces to exactly one row per source key by QUALIFY before the stage join touches it, so one source row with two pair rows at different timestamps (O3) or at the same timestamp (O4) each yielded one bridge row and one freight value. And no measure crosses an edge at all — `_stage_cte` carries only the target entity's key column, never its measures.

8. All three generated checks pass on the real warehouse (`uv run adss check`: 18/18 PASS) and all three can be made to fail. `__loaded` returned 1 for an empty pair view, 1 for pairs present only under another rel_name, and 1 for pairs all retracted; 0 once one open pair existed. `__one_target` returned 1 for one order with two open parents at a single eff_tmstp, and correctly 0 for a legitimate re-point at a later instant. `__resolves` returned 1 for a bridge key naming no row in `dar__uss.customer` (the mis-shaped M6 target), and correctly ignores a NULL key. None of the three is a check that cannot fail.

9. `entity_ids` returns ('ORDER', 'CUSTOMER') — model order, and CUSTOMER is present although it has no event, so its peripheral exists and the inherited key joins to something (89 of 91 customers appear in the bridge). Model-order fragility is finding 2.

Drift and lint. `uv run adss dar generate --check` exits 0, so the `_bridge.sql` I analysed is byte-for-byte what the generator emits; `dar build` installs the generated string rather than the file, so the warehouse cannot diverge from it either. `uv run pytest` 112 passed, `uv run ruff check` clean, `uv run sqlfluff lint checks dar` clean.

M6 conformance is enforced, not just documented: `check_relationships` runs over this repository's own `dab/mappings/*.yaml` and `dab/model.yaml` in `tests/test_relationship_rules.py:83-86`, which is in the every-commit suite. The mapping's `target_transformation_expression: customer_id` matches the CUSTOMER mapping's own `primary_keys: [customer_id]` in shape and spelling, and `source_table: das__staged.orders` is byte-identical to the group's table.

The question's own honesty holds up. `docs/questions/02-.../question.md` claims destination country and customer country coincide on all 830 orders; I verified it (0 rows differ), and confirmed the stronger consequence — rewriting `uss.sql` to read the order's own `destination_country` instead of the inherited key returns a byte-identical 153-row, 64,942.69 answer. The acceptance query therefore does not exercise the inheritance, which the question states in as many words and leans on the three data checks for instead.

result.lens: Test quality — would these tests fail if the code were wrong?
result.summary: I read every file in tests/, then copied the repo to /tmp (no .venv, no warehouse.duckdb, no das/lake) and ran 16 one-at-a-time mutations against the 112-test suite with /home/user/adss-2026-09-07/.venv/bin/python -m pytest. Nine went red, seven went green. The red ones are the prescribed list and they are genuinely good tests. The green ones are the problem: the slice's central new behaviours — that the inherited key can never fan out, and that the generated relationship checks assert anything at all — have no test that can fail, and for the fan-out case nothing downstream can catch it either, because the built warehouse contains zero pair ties (verified read-only: 0 children with more than one target at one eff_tmstp, 0 null customer_key, 830 pairs for 830 bridge rows). The machinery tests are the only line of defence for exactly the shapes the data does not yet have, and for those they assert substrings over one blob of SQL rather than the window's PARTITION BY, its ORDER BY term order, or the join conditions.

findings.where: src/adss/checks.py:153 relationship_checks() — no test anywhere in tests/
findings.finding: The three generated data checks this slice introduces (__one_target, __loaded, __resolves) come from a pure function over a data file — machinery by conventions §6's own definition — and it has zero tests. Nothing else can catch a weakened check either: `adss dar generate --check` compares the committed .sql to the same generator, so it agrees with a weakened generator; and a weakened check passes trivially at `adss check`. ADR 0006 rests its cardinality argument on this check ("the check is not optional decoration on top of the inference — it is the half of the argument the inference cannot make"), so this is the half of the argument with nothing behind it. It is also the only SQL emitter in the repo absent from tests/test_generated_sql_lints.py's `emitters()` dict (raw, staged, current, clock_check, key_check, bridge, peripheral, calendar are all there).
findings.evidence: grep -rn "relationship_checks" tests/ src/ → only src/adss/cli.py:19 and :256. Mutation: checks.py:181 `HAVING count(DISTINCT pair.{crossing(target.source_key)}) > 1` → `> 2` (a real two-parent tie is no longer counted). Result: "GREEN (suite passed) ... 112 passed". Second mutation: checks.py:205 `AND b.{target.key_column} IS NOT NULL` → `IS NULL` (the __resolves check can never count a dangling key). Result: "GREEN (suite passed)".
findings.fix: Add tests/test_relationship_checks.py over the neutral fixture model asserting each of the three emitted statements says what it exists to say (the >1 threshold, the (source_key, eff_tmstp) grouping, the NOT NULL filter and which side of the left join is tested), and add relationship_checks to test_generated_sql_lints.py's emitters dict so the new SQL is linted from the neutral fixture like every other emitter.

findings.finding: The test named for the no-fan-out property never asserts the window's PARTITION BY. Adding the target key to the partition makes row_number() return 1 for each distinct parent, so a child with two parents yields two inherit-CTE rows, two bridge rows, and doubled measures — the exact failure ADR 0006 says the bridge exists to prevent. The suite stays green, and no data check can catch it either: __one_target is a statement about the data, and today's warehouse has no tie, so the fan-out never materialises. The repo already knows how to pin this: tests/test_das_sql.py:72-73 asserts `PARTITION BY staged.parent_id` and `ORDER BY staged.extracted_at DESC` for the DAS dedup window.
findings.evidence: Mutation: uss.py:216 `f"    PARTITION BY revision.{source.key_column}\n"` → `f"    PARTITION BY revision.{source.key_column}, pair.{crossing(target.source_key)}\n"`. Result: "GREEN (suite passed) ... 112 passed". Read-only warehouse: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT "ORDER_key", eff_tmstp FROM dab."v_ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER" WHERE rel_name='ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER' AND row_st='Y' GROUP BY 1,2 HAVING count(DISTINCT "CUSTOMER_key")>1) → (0,). grep -rn "PARTITION BY" tests/ finds no assertion on the bridge at all.
findings.fix: Assert the inherit CTE's whole window verbatim, not fragments of it: extract the QUALIFY clause for one edge and compare it to the expected `PARTITION BY <source key> ORDER BY pair.eff_tmstp DESC, pair.ver_tmstp DESC, pair.<target key>` string.

findings.where: tests/test_uss.py:224 (`assert "ver_tmstp DESC" in sql`) vs src/adss/uss.py:218-219
findings.finding: ADR 0006 states the ranking is "row_number() over eff_tmstp DESC, ver_tmstp DESC". The test only asserts the substring "ver_tmstp DESC" appears somewhere in the SQL, so the two ORDER BY terms can be swapped — ranking by version timestamp before effective timestamp, which picks a different (wrong) parent whenever the two orderings disagree — and the suite is green. Today's data cannot catch it either, since every order has exactly one open pair row.
findings.evidence: Mutation: swapped uss.py:218-219 to `pair.ver_tmstp DESC,` then `pair.eff_tmstp DESC,`. Result: "GREEN (suite passed) ... 112 passed". Read-only warehouse: children with >1 open pair row = (0,), so ordering is unobservable in the build.
findings.fix: Same fix as the PARTITION BY finding — assert the ORDER BY as an ordered sequence rather than as three independent substrings.

findings.finding: The guard against a ranking function that ties is `re.search(r"(?<!row_number\(\) OVER \()\brank\s*\(", sql)`. The `\b` before `rank` does not match inside `dense_rank`, so `dense_rank()` — which ties exactly as `rank()` does — slips through, and the companion assertion `"row_number() OVER (" in sql` is still satisfied by the version CTE and the peripheral. The test that exists specifically to refuse a tying window function does not refuse one.
findings.evidence: Mutation: uss.py:215 `f"QUALIFY row_number() OVER (\n"` → `f"QUALIFY dense_rank() OVER (\n"` inside _inherit_cte only. Result: "GREEN (suite passed) ... 112 passed". (The prescribed `rank()` mutation of the same line is RED — test_the_pairs_are_ranked_deterministically_and_can_never_fan_out, tests/test_uss.py:223.)
findings.fix: Assert positively on the inherit CTE's ranking function — that the QUALIFY clause of each `<event>__<edge>` CTE opens with `row_number() OVER (` — instead of negatively excluding one spelling.

findings.finding: The test that names the slice's headline behaviour cannot tell a carried key from a typed NULL in a column of the same name. `assert "AS parent_key" in occurred` is satisfied by `cast(NULL AS VARCHAR) AS parent_key`. Two independent mutations that destroy the inheritance — emitting NULL for every inherited key, and emitting the child's own key as the parent's — both leave the suite green. ADR 0006 says all three M6 failures present as "an inherited key that is simply null everywhere, which looks like data rather than like a defect"; this is the machinery test that ought to distinguish the two, and it does not. (Both mutations are caught downstream at `adss check` — by question disagreement and by __resolves respectively — which is why this is not blocking.)
findings.evidence: Mutation A: uss.py:262 `carried = {entity.key_column} | {…edges…}` → `carried = {entity.key_column}`. Result: "GREEN (suite passed)"; the emitted CHILD branch then reads `cast(NULL AS VARCHAR) AS parent_key, occurred.child_key AS child_key, cast(NULL AS VARCHAR) AS neighbour_key`. Mutation B: uss.py:208 `pair.{crossing(target.source_key)} AS {target.key_column}` → `pair.{crossing(source.source_key)} AS {target.key_column}`. Result: "GREEN (suite passed)".
findings.fix: Assert the value, not the alias: in the branch that owns the edge, require `{event}.{target_key} AS {target_key}` and require that no `cast(NULL AS VARCHAR) AS {target_key}` appears in it; and in the inherit CTE require the selected column to be the target entity's source key.

findings.where: src/adss/uss.py:250 (the stage CTE's ON clause) — no test in tests/ references it
findings.finding: The join that attaches the inherit CTE back to the version CTE is new in this slice and its condition is asserted nowhere. Replacing it with a cross join — the most extreme fan-out available, 830 orders × 830 inherited keys, every measure multiplied 830× — leaves the machinery suite entirely green.
findings.evidence: Mutation: uss.py:250 `f"    ON {edge.id.lower()}.{entity.key_column} = revision.{entity.key_column}"` → `f"    ON TRUE"`. Result: "GREEN (suite passed) ... 112 passed". grep -rn for the CTE alias in tests/*.py returns nothing.

findings.finding: A second edge from one entity to the same target entity — or a self-edge — makes the stage CTE emit two columns with the same name, and DuckDB silently resolves the ambiguity instead of erroring, so one inherited key is dropped with nothing reporting it. ADR 0006's Consequences claim the opposite: "filtering on rel_name makes a second edge between the same two entities a new structure rather than a silent collision". The pair views are separated by rel_name; the bridge columns are not.
findings.evidence:
Both `_stage_cte` and `_branch` name an inherited key `model.entity(edge.target_entity_id).key_column`, which depends only on the target entity, never on the edge. Adding a second CHILD→PARENT edge to the neutral fixture model and calling `bridge_sql` produced:
```
occurred AS (
SELECT
    revision.child_key AS child_key,
...
    child_points_at_parent.parent_key AS parent_key,
    child_also_points_at_parent.parent_key AS parent_key,
```
and a self-edge (CHILD→CHILD) produced `revision.child_key AS child_key, ... child_follows_child.child_key AS child_key`. `formatted()` (sqlfluff, .sqlfluff config) accepted the duplicate-alias SQL — "sqlfluff ACCEPTED the duplicate-alias bridge; length 7577". DuckDB 1.5.5 then resolves it without error: `WITH s AS (SELECT a.k AS k, b.p AS p, d.p AS p FROM a LEFT JOIN b ... LEFT JOIN d ...) SELECT s.k, s.p FROM s AS s` returned `[(1, 20)]` (one of the two `p` values, silently) and `DESCRIBE` reported a single `p` column. Because `entity_keys`/`bridge_columns` dedupe by entity too, the built bridge matches its published contract and `adss check`'s first finding still passes; both edges' generated `__resolves` checks join on the one surviving column and both pass as well.
findings.fix: Refuse the model shape, or make the column name carry the edge. Cheapest: in `entity_ids`/`bridge_sql`, raise a `UssError` when `model.edges_from(e)` contains two edges with the same `target_entity_id`, or when `source_entity_id == target_entity_id`, naming ADR 0006 — the design is not decided for that case yet and a loud refusal is what ADR 0006 asks for ("a case the design cannot handle fails the build loudly rather than answering a question wrongly").

findings.evidence:

broken child mapping alone                        -> refused: bad_relationship_table.yaml: M6 -- CHILD_POINTS_AT_PARENT names source_table 'das__staged....
two CHILD mappings, broken FIRST, good LAST       -> ACCEPTED (no MappingError)

findings.finding: `key_shape()` anonymises every identifier that is not a type keyword, and a function name is an identifier — so two expressions that produce demonstrably different VARCHARs compare as the same shape and M6 accepts the pair. This is the one mechanical guard against "pairs that join to nothing", and the docstring's own reasoning ("the casting may not differ, because a bare column and a cast produce different keys") applies to functions exactly as much as to casts.
findings.evidence:
```
'left(code, 5)'      vs 'right(code, 5)'      -> SAME SHAPE (passes M6)   '?(?, 5)' | '?(?, 5)'
'upper(customer_id)' vs 'lower(customer_id)'  -> SAME SHAPE (passes M6)   '?(?)' | '?(?)'
'ltrim(code)'        vs 'rtrim(code)'         -> SAME SHAPE (passes M6)   '?(?)' | '?(?)'
'md5(code)'          vs 'sha256(code)'        -> SAME SHAPE (passes M6)   '?(?)' | '?(?)'

(run against the real `adss.mapping.key_shape`). findings.fix: Treat an identifier immediately followed by `(` as part of the shape (keep it lower-cased) rather than replacing it with `?`, so a function name survives the same way a cast does. A one-line change to the `anonymous` callback plus a lookahead in `_IDENTIFIER`.

findings.finding: `dar generate` is now a second writer into `checks/`, but only `das unpack` sweeps that directory. findings.finding: The same anonymisation false-refuses a perfectly correct mapping in three cases, and the refusal message then blames the casting, which is not what differs. Conventions §1.1 makes this reachable: DAS column names are the source's own words, and a source is free to call a column `date` or `text`.
findings.evidence:
`_SHAPE_WORDS` holds `date`, `text`, `int`, `real`, `float`, `char`, `string`, `uuid`, `decimal`, `numeric`, `double`, `timestamp`, `boolean` — all plausible column names — so a column named after one is preserved verbatim while every other column becomes `?`:
```
'cast(text AS VARCHAR)' vs 'cast(note AS VARCHAR)' -> differs (refused)
      'cast(text as varchar)' | 'cast(? as varchar)'
'date'                  vs 'order_date'            -> differs (refused)   'date' | '?'
```
`_IDENTIFIER` is ASCII-only, so `key_shape('café')` is `'?é'` against `'?'` for any plain name; and a quoted identifier containing a space is split, `key_shape('"Order Id"')` → `'"? ?"'`. All three raise the M6 error at mapping.py:257-262, whose text says "the casting may not differ".

findings.finding: The shot filename is now `question.id` with no validation, and nothing enforces that ids are unique or filename-safe. An id containing `/` or `..` escapes `.screenshots/`; an empty id falls back to `notebook.stem` AND passes `ADSS_QUESTION=""`, which the page reads as "show everything" — so that question's committed `answer.png`, the record of what was delivered, would silently be a picture of every question.

findings.finding: The page builds an answer for every question `read_questions` returns, including DRAFT and SUPERSEDED ones that `run_checks` deliberately skips, and it indexes `questions[1]` unconditionally.
